Everything the service exposes

Seven REST routes, three WebSockets, the admin socket, the ZeroMQ wire format, the embedded Python API and the CLI — with the exact parameter names, the accepted ranges, and the error code each failure returns.

Words used on this page

Status envelope — the {"status":"ok", …} or {"status":"error","error":{…}} wrapper every reply uses.
Error code — a stable machine-readable string. Match on this, never on the message.
Frame — one ZeroMQ message. Ingest and query are one part; the stream and stats sockets are two ([topic, json]).
Registry — the service's record of connections and subscriptions.
Snapshot — full state, once, on connect.
Tick — counters only, on a timer.
OpenAPI — /openapi.json, generated from the route definitions.

The routes

Seven REST routes under /api/v1, plus the pages and the WebSockets. All of it is declared in the OpenAPI schema, so a generated client cannot drift from it.

MethodPathPurpose
GET/api/v1/health Liveness. {"status":"ok","version":"0.1.0"}, or degraded when the database is not ready. Never fails on a database problem, so a load balancer can poll it safely.
POST/api/v1/write Store one measurement or a batch. Republishes to live subscribers, exactly as the ZMQ path does.
GET/api/v1/read Read a metric: raw rows, or bucketed with aggregation + interval.
GET/api/v1/aggregate Several aggregates over one window in a single pass.
GET/api/v1/stats Metric and series counts.
GET/api/v1/connections Every live WebSocket connection with its peer, topic and arrival time.
GET/api/v1/subscribers Every topic ever seen, with its live count, plus every stored metric at zero.
GET/ws/subscribe WebSocket. Live measurements for one topic.
GET/ws/connections WebSocket. One snapshot, then a frame per connect/disconnect and subscription change.
GET/ws/dashboard WebSocket. The admin dashboard feed: snapshot, live events, and a counter tick every second.
GET/ The admin dashboard page.
GET/dashboard The same page, on a path that reads well in a bookmark.
GET/dashboard-assets/* Dashboard JavaScript, CSS, icons, and the vendored Swagger and ReDoc bundles. No CDN: the gateway's own CSP forbids one.
GET/api-docs Self-hosted Swagger UI, reading /openapi.json.
GET/redoc Self-hosted ReDoc, same schema.
GET/openapi.json The machine-readable schema. The single source for a generated client.
GET/docs These pages, served by the service itself.
 
# the generated schema, straight from the route definitions
$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:12505/openapi.json | python3 -m json.tool | head -20
{
  "openapi": "3.1.0",
  "info": { "title": "sqtseries", "version": "0.1.0" },
  "paths": {
    "/api/v1/aggregate":  { … },
    "/api/v1/connections": { … },
    "/api/v1/health":     { … },
    "/api/v1/read":        { … },
    "/api/v1/stats":       { … },
    "/api/v1/subscribers": { … },
    "/api/v1/write":       { … }
  }
}

FastAPI's stock /docs page is off, because /docs serves this documentation instead and the gateway's Content-Security-Policy forbids the CDN the stock page loads from. The self-hosted equivalents are /api-docs (Swagger UI) and /redoc, both reading the same /openapi.json from vendored assets.

Every parameter, in one place

ParameterWhereTypeDefaultNotes
metricquerystring requiredMetric name. Non-empty.
startquerynumber or string null Epoch seconds over HTTP, or an ISO-8601 string. A bare numeric string is parsed as a number first.
endquerynumber or string nullInclusive.
aggregationquerystring nullOne of ten names. Unset returns raw rows.
intervalquerystring nullNs/Nm/Nh/Nd. Needs aggregation.
funcsquerystring avgComma-separated, on /aggregate only. Spaces are trimmed; empty entries dropped.
limitqueryinteger null 1–100000. Outside that is 422, checked before the handler.
orderquerystring asc asc or desc. Anything else is 422.
payloadbodyobject or array required On /write. An object is one measurement; an array is a batch, validated in full before any of it is stored.
Two different error codes for a bad parameter

It depends on who rejects it. A value the route signature declares — limit out of range, order not matching its pattern — is caught by the framework before the handler runs and comes back as 422 with a structured detail array. A value the handler checks — an unknown aggregation, a limit of 0 on the ZMQ path, an unparseable timestamp — comes back as 400 with a plain string in detail.

# 422 — rejected by the route signature
curl -s "…/api/v1/read?metric=cpu.load&limit=0"
{"detail":[{"type":"greater_than_equal","loc":["query","limit"],
  "msg":"Input should be greater than or equal to 1","ctx":{"ge":1}}]}

# 400 — rejected by the handler
curl -s "…/api/v1/read?metric=cpu.load&aggregation=bogus"
{"detail":"unsupported aggregation: bogus"}

Response shapes

# GET /api/v1/read
{"status":"ok", "data":[{"timestamp":1790793328.2546144, "value":31.0}, …]}
#   timestamp is EPOCH SECONDS even though it is stored as nanoseconds

# GET /api/v1/aggregate
{"status":"ok", "aggregations":{"avg":62.27, "p99":99.85}}
#   a function with no value is null, not 0

# POST /api/v1/write
{"status":"ok", "written":3}

# GET /api/v1/health — never fails, so a load balancer can poll it
{"status":"ok", "version":"0.1.0"}
{"status":"degraded", "version":"0.1.0"}

# GET /api/v1/stats
{"status":"ok", "metrics":2, "series":12}

# GET /api/v1/subscribers
{"status":"ok", "zmq_subscribers":0, "topics":[
  {"topic":"temp.outside", "subscribers":0, "first_seen":null, "total":null}]}

A stored metric nobody subscribes to still appears in topics, with subscribers: 0. That is deliberate: a zero row and a missing row are different facts when you are working out whether a producer stopped.

The write body is validated as a unit

Send a JSON array and the whole array is checked before any of it is stored. One bad item rejects the batch with 400 and nothing is written, so a retry is safe — there is no half-applied batch to reconcile.

curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:12505/api/v1/write \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '[{"metric":"cpu.load","value":0.42,"tags":{"host":"web1"}}]'
# the Content-Type header is required — see Client Libraries

Every error code

Match on the code. A client that branches on the message text will break the next time the wording improves.

CodeWhereMeaning
INVALID_REQUESTZMQ query/admin The frame was not a valid message object, or an admin cmd was not a string.
INVALID_QUERYZMQ query The message parsed but the query is wrong: an unknown aggregation, a bad limit, a missing metric. Distinct from INTERNAL_ERROR so a client bug is never reported as a server fault.
QUERY_TIMEOUTZMQ query The handler exceeded query.timeout_s.
MAX_ROWS_EXCEEDEDZMQ query The result would exceed query.max_rows. Narrow the window, add an aggregation, or raise the cap.
INTERNAL_ERRORZMQ query An unexpected failure. The detail is in the log, not the reply.
NOT_READYZMQ query/admin The engine is not available yet, or not at all.
BACKUP_FAILEDZMQ admin VACUUM INTO failed.
VACUUM_BUSYZMQ admin A VACUUM was refused because the database is in use. The message says to stop the service and use sqtseries vacuum.
RATE_LIMITEDHTTP 429 Over http.rate_limit_per_minute for this peer in the current one-minute window.
400HTTP Bad input: missing or empty metric, a non-numeric or non-finite value, tags that are not string-to-string, an unparseable timestamp, a timestamp outside signed 64-bit nanoseconds, or a client timestamp beyond the clock-skew window.
413HTTP The result exceeds query.max_rows. The request was valid; the answer is too big to produce under the bounded-work policy.
504HTTP The query exceeded query.timeout_s.

What each one looks like

# ZMQ — one-part reply, status envelope either way
{"status":"error", "error":{"code":"INVALID_QUERY", "message":"unsupported aggregation: bogus"}}
{"status":"error", "error":{"code":"INVALID_QUERY", "message":"limit must be a positive integer"}}
{"status":"error", "error":{"code":"INVALID_QUERY", "message":"either metric or series_ids required"}}
{"status":"error", "error":{"code":"INVALID_QUERY", "message":"timestamp not ISO-8601: 'not-a-time'"}}
{"status":"error", "error":{"code":"MAX_ROWS_EXCEEDED", "message":"query would materialize more than max_rows=10000 raw rows; …"}}
{"status":"error", "error":{"code":"INVALID_REQUEST", "message":"invalid JSON: unexpected character: line 1 column 2 (char 1)"}}
{"status":"error", "error":{"code":"INVALID_REQUEST", "message":"unknown admin command: nope"}}

# HTTP — detail is a string for handler errors, an array for schema errors
{"detail":"metric must be a non-empty string"}                    # 400
{"detail":"tags must be string->string object"}                 # 400
{"detail":"client timestamp skew exceeds 300.0s"}                   # 400
{"detail":"query would materialize more than max_rows=10000 raw rows; …"} # 413
{"detail":"query exceeded 30.0s"}                                  # 504
{"detail":[{"type":"string_pattern_mismatch", …}]}                # 422
{"status":"error","error":{"code":"RATE_LIMITED",…}}  # 429
413 and 504 mean what they say here

413 is not "your payload was too large" — the request was valid and it is the result that exceeds the bounded-work policy. 504 is the query timeout, and the query keeps running in the background; its result is discarded.

Both are the bounded-queue doctrine applied to reads: the cap exists so one query cannot make the service's memory grow with the size of the database, and it is better to refuse loudly than to answer with a plausible subset.

The admin socket

Port 12504, one request and one reply. {"cmd": "…"} in, a status envelope out. This is the surface to use from a monitoring script: it needs no HTTP client and no WebSocket, and it answers operational questions the REST API does not.

CommandRequestReply
ping{"cmd":"ping"} {"status":"ok","pong":true}
health{"cmd":"health"} Uptime, database reachability, WAL size.
stats{"cmd":"stats"} Every service counter. See the field table below.
connections{"cmd":"connections"} Every live WebSocket connection.
conncheck{"cmd":"conncheck","ids":["a","b"]} {"status":"ok","present":["a"]} — which of the given ids are still connected. An empty ids is valid and returns an empty list.
subscribers{"cmd":"subscribers"} ZMQ subscriber total plus the merged topic list.
optimize{"cmd":"optimize"} {"status":"ok","optimized":true}
backup{"cmd":"backup"} The path written, or BACKUP_FAILED.
vacuum{"cmd":"vacuum"} {"status":"ok","vacuumed":true}, or VACUUM_BUSY telling you to stop the service. The admin socket has no handler timeout, because a large backup legitimately runs long — but it holds the single SQLite writer, so ingest pauses for the duration. Use the offline CLI for anything big.

Any other cmd is refused with INVALID_REQUEST. Admin commands are not rate-limited and not authenticated: the socket binds loopback only, and that binding is the access control.

# every command, against a running service
$PY
>>> from sqtseries import Client
>>> c = Client()

>>> c.admin("ping")
{'status': 'ok', 'pong': True}

>>> c.admin("health")
{'status': 'ok', 'version': '0.1.0', 'uptime': 222, 'database': True}

>>> c.admin("connections")
{'status': 'ok', 'data': []}

>>> c.admin("subscribers")
{'status': 'ok', 'zmq_subscribers': 0, 'topics': []}

>>> c.admin("conncheck", ids=["abc", "xyz"])
{'status': 'ok', 'present': []}   # neither id is connected

>>> c.admin("nope")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
sqtseries.client.ClientError: unknown admin command: nope

The bundled Client raises ClientError with the message; over raw ZMQ you get the envelope and check status yourself.

What stats returns

29 fields. Every one is a monotonic counter except the two that are gauges, and the two you should alert on are dropped and invalid.

FieldMeans
uptime_sSeconds since the service started.
ingestedPoints accepted for storage, from both transports. recv over ZMQ plus HTTP writes.
persistedPoints actually committed. The difference from ingested is work still in flight.
droppedPoints in a batch whose insert failed after every retry. Counted, never silent — the batch is dropped whole and visible here. A transient SQLite error (a locked database, a momentary I/O fault) is retried first, so a non-zero sink_retries with dropped: 0 means the retry saved data that would otherwise have been lost.
sink_retriesBatches re-run after a transient sqlite3.OperationalError. The ZeroMQ ingest socket has no acknowledgements, so once a frame is drained the producer cannot re-send it — retrying is the only way a momentary failure does not destroy accepted data. A climbing count is an early warning for a failing disk.
invalidFrames refused as malformed or as breaching the clock-skew window.
ingest_errorsSocket-level receive errors.
queriesQuery requests served, both transports.
query_errorsHandler exceptions.
queries_shedRequests left in the socket pipe because max_inflight was reached. Backpressure made visible.
replies_droppedReplies that found no peer. The requester had already gone; counted rather than lost quietly.
admin_requestsAdmin commands served.
publishedPublish attempts, not deliveries. A slow subscriber's frame is still counted here, so this is never a per-subscriber receipt.
subscribersActive stream topics.
seriesDistinct (metric, tags) pairs.
metricsDistinct metric names.
wal_bytesCurrent WAL size.
checkpointsCheckpoints completed.
checkpoint_busy_runsCheckpoint attempts blocked by a long reader. A number that keeps climbing means something is holding a read snapshot open.
analyze_runsANALYZE passes completed.
retention_runsRetention passes completed.
partitions_droppedPartitions dropped by retention, since start.
backup_runsBackup passes, including ones that found a fresh snapshot already present.
backups_createdSnapshots actually written.
last_backupPath of the most recent snapshot.
query_cache_sizeEntries held.
query_cache_hitsQueries served from cache.
query_cache_missesQueries that had to run. A low hit rate with a busy dashboard usually means the polling interval is longer than the cache TTL.

Measured keys from a live service: status, uptime_s, ingested, invalid, ingest_errors, persisted, dropped, queries, query_errors, queries_shed, replies_dropped, admin_requests, wal_bytes, checkpoint_busy_runs, checkpoints, analyze_runs, retention_runs, partitions_dropped, backup_runs, backups_created, published, subscribers, series, metrics, query_cache_size, query_cache_hits, query_cache_misses. last_backup appears once the first snapshot has run.

The WebSocket protocols

/ws/subscribe?metric=…

Live measurements for one topic pattern. Push only: inbound frames are consumed and ignored, but consuming them is what makes a disconnect surface at once instead of at the next send.

{"metric": "cpu.load", "tags": {"host": "web1"}, "value": 0.42}
{"type": "ping"}   # after 30 s of silence — the stream is alive, there is just no data

Pattern matching is boundary aware: * takes everything, cpu. is a plain prefix, and cpu matches cpu.load but not cpu10. Full rules on Streaming.

/ws/connections

One snapshot, then a frame per change. Event-driven, with no polling.

{"type": "snapshot", "ws_connections": 2, "zmq_subscribers": 1,
 "connections": [{"id": "a1b2c3d4e5f6", "kind": "ws", "peer": "10.0.0.7:52344", "topic": "cpu."}],
 "topics": [{"topic": "cpu.load", "subscribers": 1, "first_seen": 1790786862.85}]}

{"type": "conn", "id": "a1b2c3d4e5f6", "kind": "ws", "peer": "10.0.0.7:52344",
 "topic": "cpu.", "connected": true, "connected_at": 1790786862.85, "ttl": 60}

{"type": "conn", "id": "a1b2c3d4e5f6", "connected": false,
 "connected_at": 1790786862.85, "left_at": 1790787162.90}

{"type": "sub", "kind": "zmq", "topic": "cpu.load",
 "subscribers": 2, "arrived_at": 1790786900.1, "ttl": 30}

{"type": "sub", "topic": "cpu.load", "subscribers": 1,
 "left_at": 1790786960.2, "first_seen": 1790786862.85}

/ws/dashboard

Snapshot, live events, then a counter tick every second. The tick omits the list-shaped keys, because every change in those lists already arrives as an event.

{"type": "snapshot", "status": "ok", "uptime_s": 412.7, "ingested": 40218,
 "persisted": 40218, "dropped": 0, "invalid": 0, "series": 3,
 "db_bytes": 86016, "partitions": 1, "rollup_watermark": 1790784000000000000,
 "ports": {"ingest": 12500, "query": 12502, "streaming": 12503,
              "admin": 12504, "http": 12505, "stats": 12506},
 "connections": [ … ], "topics": [ … ]}

{"type": "tick", "uptime_s": 413.7, "ingested": 40318,
 "persisted": 40318, "queries": 91, "db_bytes": 88128, …}

Close codes

CodeMeaningWhat to do
1008streaming or the registry is unavailable check the service, not the client
1009an inbound frame exceeded 16 MiB you are sending to a push-only socket
1011fan-out unavailable, or the client was too slow to flush a frame within 30 sread faster, or reconnect
1013the connection budget is exhausted back off; do not reconnect in a tight loop

The ZeroMQ wire format

One shape, three transports. Ingest and query are single-part frames; the stream and stats sockets are two-part, [topic, json], so a subscription filter works in the socket rather than in your loop.

Ingest

FieldTypeRequiredDefaultRule
metricstringyes— Non-empty. The name of the thing being measured.
valuenumberyes— Must be finite. A boolean is rejected even though Python treats it as an integer.
tagsobjectno null String keys to string values, all of them. The pairs form the series identity: the same metric with different tags is a different series.
timestampnumber or ISO-8601 string noserver clock Epoch seconds, or an ISO-8601 string with up to nanosecond precision. Outside the clock-skew window is refused. Server-assigned timestamps are forced strictly increasing, so a burst can never collide on the primary key.

Query

FieldTypeDefaultRule
metricstringrequired Non-empty.
startinteger ns or ISO-8601null Over ZMQ this is epoch nanoseconds, not seconds. The HTTP route takes seconds. A string is converted before validation.
endinteger ns or ISO-8601null Inclusive bound.
aggregationstringnull One of the ten names. Unset returns raw rows.
intervalstringnull Bucket width, Ns/Nm/Nh/Nd. Needs aggregation: alone it does nothing.
aggregationscomma-separated string null Several functions in one pass. Wins over aggregation.
limitintegernull Must be ≥ 1. On a raw read it bounds the SQL fetch; with an aggregation it bounds the number of result rows, because the transform still needs every row in the window.
orderasc or desc asc Result order.
fill_gaps_nsinteger nsnull Embedded Python API only. Inserts an interpolated midpoint across gaps no larger than this.
The units difference, one last time

Over ZMQ the query message takes epoch nanoseconds as an integer. Over HTTP the same field takes epoch seconds. Both return seconds. Getting it wrong yields an empty result with no error, so it is worth stating plainly even though it is the third time on these pages.

Admin

{"cmd": "…"} in, the same status envelope out. All nine commands are in the table above.

Stream and stats

# stream, port 12503 — two-part frames
topic   = b"cpu.load"
payload = {"metric": "cpu.load", "tags": {"host": "web1"}, "value": 0.42}

# stats, port 12506 — topic is conn | sub | report
topic   = b"conn"
payload = {"kind": "ws", "id": "a1b2c3d4e5f6", "connected": True, "peer": "10.0.0.7:52344", …}

topic   = b"report"
payload = {"uptime_s": 420.1, "ws_connections": 2, "zmq_subscribers": 1, "active_topics": 1}

The embedded Python API

No sockets, no ports, no service. The same query code the service itself uses, with a store and a facade constructed in-process.

from sqtseries.engine import StorageEngine, create_sqlite_engine, run_migrations
from sqtseries import TimeSeriesDB
import time

engine = create_sqlite_engine("/tmp/embedded.sqlite")
run_migrations(engine)                       # create the schema if new
db = TimeSeriesDB(StorageEngine(engine), max_rows=10000)
MethodArgumentsReturns
insertmetric, value, tags=None, timestamp_ns=None rows inserted
query metric=None, series_ids=None, start=None, end=None, *, aggregation=None, interval=None, limit=None, order="asc", fill_gaps_ns=None [(timestamp_ns, value), …]
query_streammetric, start=None, end=None, *, order="asc" an iterator — bounded memory over any window
aggregatemetric, start=None, end=None, *, funcs=None {func: value}
downsamplemetric, start=None, end=None, *, interval="5m", aggregation="avg" [(timestamp_ns, value), …]

start and end accept nanoseconds or an ISO-8601 string. Returns are nanoseconds — there is no gateway here to convert them.

Two things only the embedded API can do

  • query_stream — yields rows without ever holding the whole result in memory, so a month-long scan costs one row of memory.
  • fill_gaps_ns — inserts an interpolated midpoint across gaps no larger than the given size. It is not on the wire because a row you interpolated is not a row anybody measured.

To query by series identity rather than by metric name, resolve the ids first — useful when a metric has many tag sets and you want one of them:

>>> store = StorageEngine(engine)
>>> sids = store.series_ids_for_metric("cpu.load")
>>> db.query(series_ids=[sids[0]], limit=5)

The CLI

Eleven commands and two global flags. The full table, with what each needs, is on Configuration; this is the shape of it.

$ sqtseries --config PATH --db PATH COMMAND

# lifecycle
sqtseries run                 # foreground; prints the links
sqtseries stop                # SIGTERM, then wait for exit

# inspection
sqtseries status              # pid, version, real ports, links
sqtseries ports               # the ports actually bound
sqtseries health              # quick_check; exit 0 or 1
sqtseries stats               # metric and series counts

# maintenance
sqtseries backup              # VACUUM INTO snapshot
sqtseries optimize            # PRAGMA optimize
sqtseries vacuum              # full VACUUM; stop the service first

# service unit
sqtseries install             # add --system for a root unit
sqtseries uninstall
Global flags come before the subcommand

They belong to the command group, not to a command, so sqtseries --config c.toml run is correct and sqtseries run --config c.toml is an error.

Response headers

Set on every HTTP response, so a page served by the gateway inherits them:

HeaderValueWhy
X-Request-IDyour value, or 12 hex characters correlate a client report with a log line
X-Frame-OptionsDENY the API cannot be framed
X-Content-Type-Optionsnosniff no content-type guessing
Referrer-Policystrict-origin-when-cross-origin no referrer leakage to third parties
Permissions-Policy geolocation, microphone, camera, payment, usb all () the API needs none of them
Content-Security-Policy default-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data: no third-party origins at all

The /docs path is the one exception: it adds style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' so the single-file pages, whose stylesheet is inlined, render when copied elsewhere. script-src is not relaxed anywhere, and the API keeps the strict default.

One shape, three transports

An ingest message, a query request and a status envelope are the same JSON whether they travel over ZMQ, HTTP or a WebSocket. That is why this page can describe a wire format once and it stays true for every client.

The generated schema is the machine-readable half

/openapi.json comes from the FastAPI route definitions, so it cannot drift from them. If you generate a client from it, do not hand-edit the result — regenerate when the schema changes.

Errors are codes, not sentences

Every failure carries a stable machine-readable code and a human message. Match on the code. A client that branches on the message text will break when the wording improves.

Status codes that mean something specific here

413 is not a payload too large — it is a valid request whose result exceeds the bounded-work policy. 504 is the query timeout. A 429 is the per-peer rate limit, and the response says so in a body rather than only a header.

The embedded API is the same code without the sockets

TimeSeriesDB is the query facade the service itself uses. A single Python process can construct it directly and skip every port, which is the fastest possible integration and the easiest to test.

Not documented here?

The exact defaults live in the source, and the settings reference on Configuration gives each one with its key, its variable and its validation rule.

sqtseries — every route, every command, every error code.

Every default on these pages is the default in the code, checked against sqtseries --help, the live settings loader and the running service by scripts/docs-build/verify_docs.py. The wire format is the same on every transport: ZMQ PULL, ROUTER, REQ, XPUB, HTTP and WebSocket.
